name: XAT
conductingBody: XLRI – Xavier School of Management, Jamshedpur (on behalf of XAMI)
frequency: Once a year (first Sunday of January)
eligibility: Bachelor's degree (any discipline, minimum 3 years) or final-year students

notification.summary: XAT 2027 registration opened on 15 Jul 2026 on xatonline.in and is reported to remain open until about 6 Dec 2026; the computer-based exam is scheduled for Sunday 3 Jan 2027 (2–5 pm). Checked via web search on 2026-10-10 — dates are from coaching/news reports citing the official site and should be confirmed on xatonline.in.

pattern.stage: XAT (single computer-based test, Part I + Part II)
pattern.notes: Part I (Decision Making, VALR, QA-DI; 75 questions) and Part II (GK; 20 questions) — reported as 170 + 10 minutes within the 3-hour slot. Part I: +1 / −0.25, plus −0.10 for every unattempted question beyond 8. GK has no negative marking and is not counted in the XAT percentile (XLRI uses it at the final-selection stage). The essay section was discontinued from XAT 2024. Options in XAT are usually five; this mock uses four. Section-wise question counts vary slightly by year.

trendAnalysis.summary: XAT has kept a stable 3-hour format since dropping the essay in 2024, with about 75 Part I questions and 20 GK questions. QA-DI has been the toughest section in 2025 and 2026 (lengthy DI sets, algebra and geometry heavy), VALR is dominated by dense philosophical RC passages plus critical reasoning and the occasional poem, and Decision Making mixes ethical/managerial caselets with rule-based analytical sets. GK covers current affairs of the preceding year plus business and static GK and was easy in 2026. Overall difficulty: moderately difficult; time pressure and the penalty for leaving more than 8 questions make accuracy and coverage both important.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from memory-based papers and section-wise analyses of XAT 2024, XAT 2025 and XAT 2026 (held 7 Jan 2024, 5 Jan 2025 and 4 Jan 2026) by IMS, Career Launcher, TIME, Cracku, iQuanta and InsideIIM, located via web search; XLRI does not publish official papers and the full analyses could not be fetched, so recurring question types were consolidated from search snippets and the writer's own knowledge of the papers. Analyses agree on 21 DM, 26 VALR, 28 QA-DI and 20 GK questions, QA-DI as the toughest section (geometry-heavy, lengthy DI) and a poem-based item in VALR. Patterns are paraphrased; no actual question is reproduced. XAT uses five options; this mock keeps four.

archetypes.pattern: Employee discovers a safety/quality lapse that superiors want hidden; best option escalates through formal channels with evidence (not silence, not media leak, not quitting)
Conflict of interest, gifts or tainted funding; best option discloses, recuses or sets transparent conditions rather than outright rejection or quiet acceptance
Honesty vs loyalty/compassion: misreported numbers or rule-breaking by a sympathetic person; best option corrects the record while acting fairly
Strategy/operations caselet (market segments, capacity, demand peaks); choose the option that targets the actual constraint
Stakeholder trade-off under pressure from a large customer or cost cut; best option negotiates and protects compliance
Numerical decision caselet: compare alternatives by profit/contribution under given data and choose the best
Team conflict or a manager supervising former peers/friends; best first step is a private, fair conversation
Promotion, lay-off or performance decision balancing policy, fairness and individual circumstances
Rule-based eligibility set (scholarship, reimbursement, loan rules); apply all clauses to a case
Allocation of people to posts/tasks under constraints; a conditional 'if X then where is Y' question
Dense philosophical/socio-economic passage; author's main contention or central theme
Inference / author-would-agree / author's attitude on an abstract passage; options differ by degree
Role of an example or detail, or 'all of the following EXCEPT' detail check
Weaken/undermine or identify the assumption behind the passage's argument
Identify the flaw (reversed causation, correlation taken as cause) or the assumption in a short argument
Strengthen/weaken a business claim with an option that rules in or rules out alternative explanations
Deductive conclusion from conditional statements about people in an organisation
4–5 sentence para jumble with a historical or causal thread
Odd sentence out where one sentence shares the topic but not the paragraph's thread
Single/double blank vocabulary in a context sentence; logical consistency between the two blanks
Choose the grammatically correct sentence (inversion with 'Hardly/Scarcely', agreement, tense)
Short original-style poem; central idea or meaning of an image/line
Profit/discount on list price and percentage chains
Time-speed-distance: meetings, back-and-forth travel, relative speed
Work and pipes, including alternate-day work and a pipe closed midway
Mixtures and alligation (alloys, solutions)
Simple and compound interest (doubling, amounts in two years)
Algebraic identities: x + 1/x powers, a + b + c = 0 identities
Integer solutions: factor pairs, constrained non-negative solutions
Functions: functional equations, self-inverse functions, iterates
Progressions: AP/GP sums, infinite GP, Sₙ formula given
Triangle/polygon properties: angle bisector, circumradius, hexagon areas
Coordinate geometry: lines, distances, minimum areas
Mensuration of solids: cone/cylinder surface area and volume
Powers of primes in factorials, last digits and cyclicity
HCF/LCM pairs and divisibility conditions
Arrangements and distributions with restrictions (non-adjacent, at least k each)
Probability with dice, balls or selections
Table-based DI: shares, margins and comparisons where the largest absolute value is the trap
Caselet DI with what-if changes or overlapping categories
Appointments and heads of governments/institutions in the past year
Awards and prizes of the past year (Nobel, Booker, Peace)
International summits, chairships and sporting-event hosts
Economy and policy institutions: commissions, payment systems, budget announcements
Corporate news: mergers, joint ventures, brand ownership
Static geography of India
History and polity basics (battles, texts, constitutional provisions)
Science and sports facts linked to recent events

resources.notes: XLRI publishes a free official mock test for registered candidates on xatonline.in shortly before the exam. Official answer keys/question papers are not routinely published; previous papers in circulation are memory-based reconstructions by coaching institutes.

questions.question: Ritika, a quality engineer at a medical-device firm, discovers that a batch of blood-pressure monitors already shipped to hospitals gives readings that are off by up to 15 mmHg in certain conditions. Her manager says a recall would hurt the quarter's results and suggests quietly correcting the issue in the next batch. What should Ritika do?
options: Post the details anonymously on social media to force the company to act.
Follow her manager's suggestion, since the next batch will be fixed.
Escalate the issue through the firm's formal quality/compliance channel, insisting that affected hospitals be informed and the batch be corrected or recalled.
Resign immediately without informing anyone.
questions.explanation: Patient safety is at stake and the faulty devices are already in use, so silence is unacceptable. Using formal internal channels first is both responsible and effective; going public first is premature and resignation does not protect patients.

questions.question: A procurement manager, Arun, is evaluating three vendors. One vendor, whose bid is the second-cheapest, sends him an expensive smartphone as a 'Diwali gift'. Company policy prohibits gifts above ₹1,000. Which is the most appropriate action?
options: Disqualify all three vendors and restart the process.
Return the gift, inform his superior or the compliance team, and continue evaluating all bids on merit.
Accept the gift, since refusing it during a festival would be rude.
Keep the gift but make sure he still selects the cheapest vendor.
questions.explanation: Returning the gift and disclosing it keeps Arun within policy and protects the integrity of the process. Keeping it creates a conflict of interest; disqualifying the other vendors punishes those who did nothing wrong.

questions.question: A start-up's founder, Meera, learns that her best-performing salesperson inflated client numbers in a pitch deck to a large prospective customer. The deal has not yet been signed. The salesperson argues 'everyone rounds up' and that correcting it now will lose the deal. What should Meera do?
options: Fire the salesperson publicly to set an example, without informing the customer.
Withdraw from the deal without explanation.
Let the deal close and correct the numbers later if the customer asks.
Correct the figures with the prospective customer before signing and address the misconduct with the salesperson.
questions.explanation: Signing on the basis of known false figures would be misrepresentation and would endanger trust and legal standing. Correcting before signing and dealing with the employee's conduct addresses both the external and internal problems.

questions.question: During an exam at a B-school, invigilator Prof. Das notices that a student who is also a scholarship holder has a sheet of formulae under his calculator. The student pleads that he forgot it was there and that losing the scholarship would force him to drop out. What should Prof. Das do?
options: Ignore it out of sympathy for the student's financial situation.
Announce the incident to the whole class to deter others.
Tear up the student's answer script on the spot and expel him from the hall.
Confiscate the sheet, record the incident as per the institute's rules, and let the disciplinary committee decide after hearing the student.
questions.explanation: Due process — stopping the violation, documenting it and letting the designated committee decide after a hearing — balances fairness to other students with fairness to the accused. Ignoring it is unfair to others; on-the-spot punishment or public shaming bypasses due process.

questions.question: A mid-sized FMCG company finds that its new snack has strong sales in metro cities but poor sales in small towns, where a cheaper local brand dominates. Distribution costs in small towns are high. The CEO wants to grow overall profit in the next year. Which is the best course of action?
options: Cut the price sharply across all markets to beat the local brand.
Double the advertising budget in small towns immediately.
Focus resources on metros where the product is profitable, and test a smaller, lower-priced pack in a few small towns before expanding.
Withdraw the product from metros and concentrate on small towns.
questions.explanation: Concentrating on profitable markets protects margins, while a limited low-price pack test gathers evidence about small-town demand at low cost. A blanket price cut sacrifices metro margins; abandoning metros or spending heavily without evidence is risky.

questions.question: A bus operator runs a route on which the average occupancy is 90% on weekdays and 35% on weekends. Each bus costs the same to run every day. The operator wants to improve profitability without reducing service quality for weekday commuters. Which is the most sensible option?
options: Raise weekday fares sharply since demand is high.
Shut the route on weekdays.
Increase the number of weekday buses and keep weekend trips unchanged.
Reduce the number of weekend trips and offer weekend discount fares to raise occupancy on the remaining trips.
questions.explanation: Weekend trips are the loss-making part: cutting surplus weekend capacity and stimulating demand with discounts improves utilisation without touching weekday service. A sharp weekday hike risks losing commuters; adding weekday buses or closing weekdays does not address the weekend problem.

questions.question: A software firm has a key client who accounts for 45% of its revenue. The client demands a 20% price cut, threatening to move to a competitor. The firm's margins on this client are currently 25%. What should the firm's management do first?
options: Negotiate — explore a smaller discount linked to longer contract tenure or higher volume — while starting efforts to diversify the client base.
Accept the 20% cut immediately to avoid losing the client.
Lay off 20% of staff to protect margins before talking to the client.
Refuse any discount and let the client leave.
questions.explanation: Accepting would almost wipe out margins (25% → about 6%); refusing outright risks losing 45% of revenue. Negotiating a trade-off and reducing dependence on one client addresses both the immediate and the structural problem.

questions.question: A hospital's emergency department is overcrowded every evening between 6 pm and 10 pm, while it is underused in the early morning. Most evening patients have non-critical conditions. What is the best way to reduce evening overcrowding?
options: Close the emergency department in the early morning to save money.
Hire more doctors only for the early-morning shift.
Set up a triage desk and a separate fast-track area for non-critical cases during evening hours.
Turn away all non-critical patients in the evening.
questions.explanation: Triage with a fast-track stream handles the many non-critical evening cases efficiently without denying care; turning patients away is unsafe, and the morning options do nothing for evening crowding.

questions.question: Two team leads, Kabir and Sana, both claim credit for a successful product launch and have stopped cooperating. Their manager, Nisha, notices that the team is taking sides. What should Nisha do first?
options: Ask the team to vote on who deserves credit.
Announce that only Kabir will lead future launches.
Meet both of them, acknowledge their specific contributions, and agree on how future joint work and credit will be handled.
Ignore the conflict, as it will resolve itself with time.
questions.explanation: The conflict is already affecting the team, so it cannot be ignored; a public vote or unilateral choice escalates it. Recognising both contributions and setting ground rules addresses the cause.

questions.question: Imran, a new graduate trainee, is consistently ten minutes late for morning meetings. His work quality is excellent. His supervisor learns that Imran drops his younger sister at school on the way, and the school opens only at 8:45 am, while meetings start at 9:00 am at an office 25 minutes away. What should the supervisor do?
options: Ignore the issue completely because his work is good.
Issue a formal warning for repeated late-coming.
Ask him to make other arrangements for his sister immediately.
Discuss the situation with Imran and, if feasible, shift the meeting time or allow him to join the first part remotely.
questions.explanation: The cause is a genuine, structural constraint and the employee performs well; a reasonable accommodation after discussion keeps both performance and punctuality issues in view. A warning ignores context; doing nothing leaves the meeting problem unresolved.

questions.question: A manager, Leela, must choose one of two subordinates for a promotion. Ravi has higher sales figures, but several colleagues have complained about his aggressive behaviour. Pooja has slightly lower sales but is consistently rated highly by peers and clients for teamwork. The new role involves leading a team of eight. Whom should Leela promote, and why?
options: Neither, to avoid upsetting either of them.
Ravi, but only after asking Pooja whether she objects.
Pooja, because the role is about leading a team and her teamwork record is more relevant than a small sales difference.
Ravi, because sales figures are the only objective measure.
questions.explanation: Promotion should match the demands of the new role. Leading eight people depends heavily on interpersonal skills, where Pooja is stronger and Ravi has complaints; the sales gap is small.

questions.question:
A foundation awards scholarships using these rules:
(1) The applicant must have scored at least 75% in the qualifying exam.
(2) Annual family income must be below ₹6 lakh; however, if the applicant is a first-generation graduate, income up to ₹8 lakh is acceptable.
(3) The applicant must not be receiving any other scholarship.
Applicants: Ajay — 78%, income ₹7 lakh, first-generation graduate, no other scholarship. Bina — 82%, income ₹5 lakh, receives a state scholarship. Chetan — 74%, income ₹3 lakh, no other scholarship. Dia — 76%, income ₹7.5 lakh, not first-generation, no other scholarship.

Who is eligible?
options: Only Ajay
Ajay and Bina
Ajay, Chetan and Dia
Ajay and Dia
questions.explanation: Ajay: 78% ✓, ₹7 lakh allowed as first-generation ✓, no other scholarship ✓ → eligible. Bina fails rule 3; Chetan fails rule 1 (74%); Dia fails rule 2 (₹7.5 lakh without first-generation status). Only Ajay.

questions.question:
A company reimburses travel as follows:
• Train travel is always reimbursed.
• Air travel is reimbursed only if the journey exceeds 800 km, or if the employee is at manager level or above.
• Taxi fares within the city are reimbursed up to ₹1,500 per trip; anything above is not reimbursed.
Neha, an executive (below manager level), flew 650 km to a client meeting and took one city taxi costing ₹1,900. What amount of these two expenses is reimbursable?
options: The full flight and the full taxi fare
Only ₹1,500 of the taxi fare; the flight is not reimbursable
Nothing at all
The full flight and ₹1,500 of the taxi fare
questions.explanation: The flight (650 km, non-manager) meets neither air-travel condition. The taxi is reimbursed up to the ₹1,500 cap, so ₹1,500 is reimbursable.

questions.question:
A bank's loan policy:
(i) The applicant must be aged 21–60.
(ii) The proposed EMI must not exceed 40% of monthly income.
(iii) Applicants with a credit score below 650 are rejected; those with 650–699 need a guarantor; those with 700 or above need no guarantor.
Mohan, aged 45, earns ₹80,000 a month, has a credit score of 680 and applies for a loan with an EMI of ₹30,000. He has a guarantor ready. What is the correct decision?
options: Approve without a guarantor.
Reject, because the EMI exceeds 40% of his income.
Approve the loan with Mohan's guarantor.
Reject, because his credit score is below 700.
questions.explanation: Age 45 ✓. EMI ₹30,000 = 37.5% of ₹80,000 ≤ 40% ✓. Score 680 lies in 650–699, so a guarantor is required, and he has one. Hence approve with the guarantor.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"We tend to think of freedom as the absence of constraint, as if the freest person were the one with the fewest rules. Yet the pianist who can improvise freely has spent years submitting to scales, and the speaker who can say anything has first accepted the rigid grammar of a language. Constraint, rightly chosen, is not the opposite of freedom but its precondition: it builds the capacities without which choice is empty."

The author's main contention is that:
options: musicians are freer than other people
certain disciplines enlarge rather than diminish a person's real freedom
freedom is merely an illusion created by rules
all rules should be accepted without question
questions.explanation: The examples of the pianist and the speaker support the claim that 'rightly chosen' constraint builds the capacities that make freedom meaningful. The author does not say freedom is an illusion or that all rules must be accepted.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Gift economies are often romanticised as systems of pure generosity. Anthropologists have long noted, however, that a gift creates an obligation: to accept, to reciprocate, and often to reciprocate more lavishly. The giver gains not wealth but standing. In this sense the gift is not the opposite of the market but a different way of keeping accounts—one denominated in honour rather than coin."

Which of the following would the author most likely agree with?
options: Gift economies are free of any expectation of return.
Gift-giving can serve as a means of building status and social obligation.
Anthropologists have failed to study gift economies.
Markets are more honourable than gift economies.
questions.explanation: The author says gifts create obligations and that the giver gains 'standing' — a system of accounting 'in honour'. This rejects the 'pure generosity' view and makes no comparison of honour between markets and gifts.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Early photographs required exposures of many minutes, and so the streets in them appear eerily empty: carriages and pedestrians moved too quickly to register. Only a man who stopped to have his boots polished stood still long enough to be recorded. The camera, which we imagine as a faithful witness, was in its infancy a witness only to stillness."

The example of the man having his boots polished is used to show that:
options: early cameras could record only subjects that remained still for a long time
early photographers deliberately avoided crowds
boot-polishing was a popular trade at the time
streets in the nineteenth century were usually empty
questions.explanation: Because exposures took minutes, only stationary subjects appeared; the man appears because he stood still. The streets were not actually empty — moving people simply did not register.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The expert's advantage lies less in knowing more facts than in knowing which facts matter. A novice chess player sees thirty-two pieces; a master sees three or four meaningful patterns. This compression is a gift and a trap: it allows rapid judgement, but it also makes the expert slow to notice when a familiar-looking situation is in fact new."

The passage suggests that expertise:
options: speeds judgement but can make one miss genuine novelty
consists mainly of memorising more facts than a novice
is irrelevant in games like chess
makes errors impossible in familiar situations
questions.explanation: The author says compression is 'a gift and a trap': rapid judgement, but slowness to notice that a familiar-looking situation is new. The first sentence explicitly denies that expertise is mainly about more facts.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Cities that grew up around rivers often turned their backs on them during industrialisation, lining the banks with warehouses, drains and roads. Recent decades have seen a reversal: promenades, parks and cafés now crowd onto waterfronts once considered fit only for sewage. Yet the reclaimed riverbank is frequently priced beyond the reach of those who lived beside the river when it stank."

The final sentence of the passage introduces:
options: a proposal to restore warehouses on riverbanks
a concern about who benefits from the revival of waterfronts
evidence that waterfront parks are unpopular
a reason why industrial cities ignored their rivers
questions.explanation: After describing the revival, the author notes that the improved riverbank is often unaffordable for earlier residents — a concern about the distribution of benefits.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"A rule that is never enforced does not merely fail; it teaches. It instructs everyone who observes its neglect that the institution's words and its intentions are different things. The cost is not limited to the rule in question: every other rule is quietly discounted as well."

Which of the following is the most appropriate inference from the passage?
options: Unenforced rules can weaken the credibility of an institution's other rules.
Rules are effective only if they are written clearly.
Most people do not notice whether rules are enforced.
Institutions should have fewer rules.
questions.explanation: The passage says neglect of one rule leads people to 'discount' every other rule — a loss of credibility. It does not prescribe fewer rules or discuss clarity.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Folk remedies are frequently dismissed as superstition, and many deserve to be. But several modern medicines began as plants used by healers whose explanations were wrong even when their results were right. The task of science is neither to embrace tradition wholesale nor to dismiss it, but to test it."

The author's attitude towards folk remedies is best described as:
options: open-minded but insistent on testing
uncritically admiring
indifferent
wholly dismissive
questions.explanation: The author concedes that many deserve dismissal but notes some led to real medicines, concluding that tradition should be tested — neither embraced nor dismissed.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"When a company boasts that its new product is 'disruptive', it usually means that it is popular. But disruption, in the stricter sense, describes something less flattering: a cheaper, initially inferior offering that established firms ignore because their best customers do not want it, until it improves enough to take those customers away."

According to the passage, in the stricter sense, a disruptive product:
options: is one that established firms quickly copy
is any product that becomes very popular
typically starts as a cheaper, lower-quality offering that incumbents overlook
is always superior to existing products from the start
questions.explanation: The passage defines strict disruption as a cheaper, initially inferior offering ignored by established firms until it improves — not mere popularity or initial superiority.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Handwritten letters survive in archives in a way that emails seldom do. Historians of our era may therefore face an odd problem: not too little evidence, but too much of the wrong kind—billions of messages stored on servers that may be inaccessible, unreadable or deleted, alongside a thinning trickle of paper."

What 'odd problem' does the passage anticipate for future historians?
options: There will be no written records of the present era.
Evidence may be abundant in volume yet hard to access or preserve.
Emails contain no historically useful information.
Handwritten letters will be too numerous to study.
questions.explanation: The problem is 'not too little evidence, but too much of the wrong kind' — vast digital records that may be inaccessible or lost.

questions.question:
"Our firm's employee survey shows that staff who use the office gym report higher job satisfaction. So, to raise satisfaction, we should make gym use compulsory."

Which of the following identifies the main flaw in this reasoning?
options: It assumes gym use causes satisfaction, when already-satisfied employees may simply be more likely to use the gym.
It ignores the cost of building a gym.
It relies on a survey of employees.
It assumes that all employees like exercise.
questions.explanation: A correlation between gym use and satisfaction is treated as causation; the direction may be reversed, or a third factor (e.g. flexible schedules) may explain both.

questions.question:
"Sales of umbrellas in the city rose by 40% this year. Therefore, it must have rained more this year than last year."

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the conclusion?
options: Umbrella sales in the city have risen every year for a decade.
A popular retailer began selling umbrellas at half the usual price this year.
Rainfall is measured at several stations across the city.
Most umbrellas are bought during the monsoon months.
questions.explanation: A large price cut offers an alternative explanation for the rise in sales that has nothing to do with rainfall.

questions.question:
Arrange the sentences into a coherent paragraph.

1. These marks, called 'hallmarks', guaranteed the purity of the metal to any buyer.
2. In medieval London, goldsmiths had to bring their work to a guild hall to be tested.
3. Today the word has come to mean any distinctive feature of a person or thing.
4. If the item passed, it was stamped with a set of official marks.
questions.explanation: 2 sets the scene (testing at the guild hall); 4 says what happened if the item passed; 1 names these marks and their purpose; 3 describes the word's modern extended meaning.

questions.question:
"The new metro line will reduce congestion on the city's main arterial road, because many commuters who now drive along it will switch to the metro."

Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
options: The metro will be cheaper to build than widening the road.
Metro fares will be the lowest in the country.
The metro line connects the places that drivers on the arterial road actually travel between.
Everyone in the city owns a car.
questions.explanation: Drivers will switch only if the metro serves their actual journeys; if it did not, the predicted switch — and the congestion relief — would not follow. The other options are not required by the argument.

questions.question:
Five sentences are given. Four form a coherent paragraph. Identify the one that does NOT belong.

1. Mangrove forests grow in the salty, oxygen-poor mud of tropical coastlines.
2. Their tangled roots trap sediment and slow the force of incoming waves.
3. As a result, coasts fringed by mangroves often suffer less damage during cyclones.
4. Coral reefs are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth.
5. Mangroves also shelter juvenile fish, making them important to coastal fisheries.
options: Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 5
Sentence 2
questions.explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 describe mangroves and their protective and ecological roles. Sentence 4 abruptly switches to coral reefs.

questions.question:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.

"The CEO's ______ manner—she rarely spoke in meetings and never raised her voice—led new employees to underestimate her, until they saw how decisively she acted."
options: bombastic
frivolous
garrulous
reticent
questions.explanation: She 'rarely spoke' and was quiet, so 'reticent' (reserved) fits. 'Garrulous' and 'bombastic' mean talkative/pompous; 'frivolous' does not fit the description.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Each of the candidates has submitted the required documents.
Each of the candidates have submitted the required documents.
Each of the candidate has submitted the required documents.
Each of the candidates have submit the required documents.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular and takes 'has'; 'of the' must be followed by the plural 'candidates'; the past participle is 'submitted'.

questions.question:
Read the poem and answer the question.

"The old well in the courtyard
has forgotten the bucket and the rope;
it keeps instead a circle of sky
and, at noon, one burning coin of sun.
Children lean over and shout their names—
the well returns them, a little slower,
as if it had to look them up."

Which of the following best describes the central idea of the poem?
options: A disused well, no longer serving its practical purpose, has taken on a quieter, almost living presence.
The well is dangerous and should be sealed to protect children.
Water scarcity has made the village abandon its well.
Children have forgotten how to use a bucket and rope.
questions.explanation: The well 'has forgotten the bucket and the rope' (no longer used) but now 'keeps' sky and sun and 'returns' children's names as if remembering them — personification of a disused object with a new, gentle life. Nothing suggests danger or scarcity.

questions.question: A shopkeeper sells two items for ₹1,200 each. On one he gains 20% and on the other he loses 20%. What is his overall result?
options: Loss of 4%
Gain of 4%
Loss of 2%
No profit, no loss

questions.question: Pipe A fills a tank in 12 hours and pipe B in 15 hours; pipe C empties the full tank in 20 hours. All three are opened together on an empty tank, and C is closed after 5 hours. How long does it take in all to fill the tank?
options: 7 hours 40 minutes
8 hours
9 hours
8 hours 20 minutes
questions.explanation: Net rate of all three = 1/12 + 1/15 − 1/20 = (5 + 4 − 3)/60 = 1/10. In 5 hours: half full. A + B fill 9/60 = 3/20 per hour, so the remaining 1/2 takes 10/3 h = 3 h 20 min. Total 8 h 20 min.

questions.question: Two cyclists start at the same time from towns P and Q, 90 km apart, riding towards each other at 20 km/h and 25 km/h respectively. Each, on reaching the other town, turns back immediately at the same speed. How far from P do they meet for the second time?
options: 30 km
45 km
72 km
60 km
questions.explanation: By the second meeting they have together covered 3 × 90 = 270 km, taking 270/45 = 6 hours. The cyclist from P has ridden 120 km: 90 km to Q and 30 km back, i.e. 60 km from P.

questions.question: Alloy A contains copper and zinc in the ratio 3 : 2, and alloy B contains them in the ratio 1 : 3. In what ratio (by weight) must A and B be mixed so that the new alloy has equal amounts of copper and zinc?
questions.explanation: Copper fractions: A = 0.6, B = 0.25, target 0.5. By alligation, A : B = (0.5 − 0.25) : (0.6 − 0.5) = 0.25 : 0.10 = 5 : 2.

questions.question: A sum of money doubles in 6 years at compound interest (compounded annually at a fixed rate). In how many years will it become eight times itself?
questions.explanation: 8 = 2³, so it takes three doubling periods: 3 × 6 = 18 years.

questions.question: If x + 1/x = 3, what is the value of x⁵ + 1/x⁵?
How many ordered pairs of integers (x, y) satisfy x² − y² = 45?
questions.explanation: (x − y)(x + y) = 45. Both factors must have the same parity; since 45 is odd, all its factor pairs are odd. Ordered factor pairs (a, b) with ab = 45: (1, 45), (3, 15), (5, 9), (9, 5), (15, 3), (45, 1) and their negatives — 12 pairs, each giving integer x = (a + b)/2, y = (b − a)/2. So 12.

questions.question: A function f satisfies f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x for every non-zero real x. What is f(2)?
The sum of an infinite geometric progression is 20, and the sum of the squares of its terms is 100. What is the first term?
A triangle has sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. What is the radius of its circumcircle?
options: 7.5 cm
8 cm
8.5 cm

questions.question: In a regular hexagon of side 6 cm, alternate vertices are joined to form a triangle. What is the area of this triangle?
options: 54√3 cm²
27√3 cm²
36√3 cm²
18√3 cm²
questions.explanation: The distance between alternate vertices of a regular hexagon with side a is a√3 = 6√3. Equilateral-triangle area = (√3/4)(6√3)² = (√3/4)(108) = 27√3 cm² (exactly half the hexagon's 54√3).

questions.question: A straight line passes through the point (2, 3) and cuts the positive x-axis and the positive y-axis. What is the minimum possible area of the triangle it forms with the coordinate axes?
questions.explanation: Line x/a + y/b = 1 with 2/a + 3/b = 1. By AM–GM, 1 = 2/a + 3/b ≥ 2√(6/(ab)), so ab ≥ 24 and the area ab/2 ≥ 12, with equality when 2/a = 3/b = 1/2, i.e. a = 4, b = 6.

questions.question: What is the highest power of 3 that divides 50! exactly?
What are the last two digits of 7²⁰²⁶?
Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is a prime number?
In how many ways can 8 identical chocolates be distributed among 3 children so that each child gets at least 2?
questions.explanation: Give 2 to each first; 2 chocolates remain to be distributed freely among 3 children: C(2 + 2, 2) = 6.

questions.question:
A company's sales (₹ lakh) by region and product are:

Region | P | Q | R
North | 120 | 80 | 50
South | 90 | 110 | 70
East | 60 | 40 | 100
West | 130 | 70 | 60

In which region does product R account for the largest share of that region's total sales?
options: West
East
North
South

questions.question:
A company's sales (₹ lakh) by region and product are:

Region | P | Q | R
North | 120 | 80 | 50
South | 90 | 110 | 70
East | 60 | 40 | 100
West | 130 | 70 | 60

Approximately what percentage of the company's total sales comes from product P?

A company's sales (₹ lakh) by region and product are:

Region | P | Q | R
North | 120 | 80 | 50
South | 90 | 110 | 70
East | 60 | 40 | 100
West | 130 | 70 | 60

Next year, sales of every product rise by 10% in North and fall by 10% in East, while South and West are unchanged. Approximately what is the percentage change in the company's total sales?
options: A decrease of about 0.5%
An increase of about 1%
An increase of about 0.5%
No change

questions.question: Who has been the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India since December 2024?
options: Shaktikanta Das
Sanjay Malhotra
Urjit Patel
Michael Patra
questions.explanation: Sanjay Malhotra took charge as the 26th RBI Governor on 11 December 2024, succeeding Shaktikanta Das.

questions.question: The 2025 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was awarded for work on:
options: auction theory
behavioural finance
innovation-driven economic growth
poverty alleviation experiments
questions.explanation: The 2025 prize went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for explaining innovation-driven economic growth (including 'creative destruction').

questions.question: Which country holds the chairship of BRICS in 2026?
options: South Africa
Brazil
Russia
India
questions.explanation: Brazil chaired BRICS in 2025 and handed over to India, which holds the BRICS chairship for 2026.

questions.question: The UN Climate Change Conference COP30 (November 2025) was hosted by which country?
options: Azerbaijan
Brazil
United Arab Emirates
Egypt
questions.explanation: COP30 was held in Belém, Brazil. The UAE hosted COP28 (2023), Azerbaijan COP29 (2024) and Egypt COP27 (2022).

questions.question: Who became Chairperson of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in March 2025?
options: Tuhin Kanta Pandey
Ajay Tyagi
Madhabi Puri Buch
U. K. Sinha
questions.explanation: Tuhin Kanta Pandey, formerly Finance Secretary, took over as SEBI chairperson on 1 March 2025, succeeding Madhabi Puri Buch.

questions.question: The Sixteenth Finance Commission, whose recommendations cover the period 2026–27 to 2030–31, is chaired by:
options: Y. V. Reddy
N. K. Singh
Raghuram Rajan
Arvind Panagariya
questions.explanation: Arvind Panagariya chairs the 16th Finance Commission; N. K. Singh chaired the 15th and Y. V. Reddy the 14th.

questions.question: The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) was developed and is operated by:
options: National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)
Reserve Bank of India directly
Ministry of Electronics and IT
State Bank of India
questions.explanation: UPI was developed by NPCI, an umbrella organisation for retail payments promoted by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association.

questions.question: Through how many Indian states does the Tropic of Cancer pass?
options: Seven
Nine
Six
Eight
questions.explanation: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram — eight states.

questions.question: The ancient treatise on statecraft and economics, the Arthashastra, is traditionally attributed to:
options: Banabhatta
Megasthenes
Kalidasa
Kautilya (Chanakya)
questions.explanation: The Arthashastra is attributed to Kautilya, also known as Chanakya, adviser to Chandragupta Maurya.

questions.question: In December 2024, D. Gukesh became the youngest undisputed World Chess Champion by defeating whom in the title match?
options: Magnus Carlsen
Fabiano Caruana
Ding Liren
Ian Nepomniachtchi
questions.explanation: Gukesh beat China's Ding Liren 7.5–6.5 in Singapore in December 2024.

questions.question: Anand, a quality engineer at a food-processing company, finds that a batch of infant cereal already dispatched to distributors contains a preservative above the limit permitted by Indian food-safety regulations, though within limits allowed in some other countries. The plant head asks him to let the batch be sold, since a recall would cost ₹2 crore and the plant is about to receive an industry award. What should Anand do?
options: Agree with the plant head, since the levels are acceptable under some international standards.
Inform the media immediately so that parents learn of the problem.
Report the finding with the test data to the company's quality and compliance head and recommend holding and recalling the batch as the law requires.
Retest samples from the batch until a result within the permitted limit is obtained.
questions.explanation: The batch breaches the applicable Indian limit and is meant for infants, so letting it be sold is unacceptable; retesting until a pass is dishonest. Going to the media before using internal channels is premature. Formal escalation with evidence and a recommendation to hold/recall addresses both the safety risk and legal compliance.

questions.question: Priya heads procurement at a private hospital. For a large purchase of diagnostic equipment, the lowest technically compliant bid has come from a firm owned by her brother-in-law. Hospital rules require a three-member committee, of which she is the chair, to evaluate bids. What should Priya do?
options: Ask her brother-in-law to withdraw the bid quietly.
Award the contract to the firm, since its bid is objectively the lowest.
Disclose the relationship to the hospital management and withdraw from evaluating this tender, leaving the committee to decide on merit.
Reject her brother-in-law's bid to avoid any appearance of favouritism.
questions.explanation: Disclosure and recusal remove the conflict while allowing the hospital to benefit from the best bid. Rejecting a compliant lowest bid is unfair to the firm and costly to the hospital; awarding it herself leaves the conflict undisclosed; asking for a quiet withdrawal distorts the tender.

questions.question: Kiran, co-founder of a start-up, discovers that his co-founder reported monthly active users about 30% higher than the true figure to investors during a funding round that closed last month, by counting long-dormant accounts. The co-founder argues that the investors 'invested in the vision, not the number'. What should Kiran do?
options: Discuss the matter with his co-founder and then proactively inform the investors of the correct figures and the revised method of counting.
Resign without telling anyone the reason.
Stay silent, since the funding has already been received.
Sell his stake in the company quietly before the error becomes public.
questions.explanation: Investors made a decision on a materially wrong metric; correcting it promptly (after engaging the co-founder) is honest and limits legal and reputational damage. Silence perpetuates the misrepresentation, selling on undisclosed information is unethical, and resigning silently fixes nothing.

questions.question: A river-cleaning NGO is offered a large donation by a chemical company that was fined last year for discharging effluents into the same river. The money would fund three years of the NGO's work. Several volunteers threaten to quit if it is accepted. Which is the most appropriate course of action for the NGO's board?
options: Accept the donation quietly without informing volunteers or the public.
Reject the donation outright without any discussion.
Accept the donation on the condition that the NGO stops criticising the company.
Consult the volunteers and, if accepting, do so publicly under written terms that guarantee the NGO's independence, disclose the source and commit the company to remediating its own pollution.
questions.explanation: The option that consults stakeholders, preserves independence, ensures transparency and ties funding to remediation balances the mission's needs with integrity. Quiet acceptance or a gag clause compromises the NGO, while outright rejection without discussion forgoes resources and ignores stakeholders.

questions.question: A bakery sells 1,000 cakes a week at ₹400 each. The variable cost is ₹250 per cake and fixed costs are ₹90,000 a week. The owner is considering two options: (i) cut the price by 10%, which a survey suggests will raise weekly sales by 20%; or (ii) run an advertising campaign costing ₹20,000 a week, expected to raise sales by 15% at the current price. Which decision maximises weekly profit?
options: Cut the price, since it gives the larger increase in sales.
Cut the price by 10%.
Make no change, since both options reduce profit.
Run the advertising campaign.
questions.explanation: Current profit = 1,000 × 150 − 90,000 = ₹60,000. Price cut: 1,200 × (360 − 250) − 90,000 = ₹42,000. Advertising: 1,150 × 150 − 90,000 − 20,000 = ₹62,500. Advertising is the only option that raises profit.

questions.question: A garment exporter's largest buyer, accounting for 40% of revenue, demands a 15% price reduction. The production head suggests shifting part of the work to subcontractors who pay below minimum wage, which would meet the target. The buyer's code of conduct prohibits such practices, though it rarely audits. What should the exporter do?
options: Stop supplying the buyer immediately.
Shift the work to the cheaper subcontractors, since the buyer rarely audits.
Negotiate with the buyer on a smaller reduction while cutting costs through efficiencies such as reducing fabric waste, without using non-compliant subcontractors.
Accept the full price cut and absorb the loss.
questions.explanation: Using underpaying subcontractors is illegal and breaches the buyer's code—an unacceptable risk even if audits are rare. Absorbing the full cut or walking away abandons a 40% customer without exploring options. Negotiation combined with genuine efficiency gains addresses the pressure responsibly.

questions.question: An FMCG company's new premium shampoo sells well in metros in 400 ml bottles. In rural markets, sales are negligible: retailers say customers buy shampoo in single-use sachets and the large bottle ties up too much of their working capital. What should the company do to grow rural sales?
options: Withdraw the product from rural markets.
Cut the price of the 400 ml bottle in rural markets.
Increase rural advertising for the 400 ml bottle.
Launch the shampoo in low-priced sachets for rural distribution, with retailer margins suited to small packs.
questions.explanation: The constraint is pack size and retailer working capital, not awareness or price per millilitre. Sachets match rural buying habits and are easy for retailers to stock. Price cuts or advertising for the bottle do not remove the constraint; withdrawal gives up the market.

questions.question: A factory makes two products. Product X earns a profit of ₹40 per unit and needs 2 machine-hours; product Y earns ₹50 per unit and needs 4 machine-hours. 400 machine-hours are available each week, and at most 150 units of X and 100 units of Y can be sold per week. Which weekly production plan maximises profit?
options: 50 units of X and 75 units of Y
150 units of X only
150 units of X and 25 units of Y
100 units of X and 50 units of Y
questions.explanation: X earns ₹20 per machine-hour and Y ₹12.5, so make the maximum 150 X (300 hours) and use the remaining 100 hours for 25 Y: profit 6,000 + 1,250 = ₹7,250. The other plans give ₹6,500, ₹5,750 and ₹6,000.

questions.question: Meghna has just been promoted to manage the team she was part of. Arjun, a close friend in the team, has started arriving 30–40 minutes late most days, and other members have begun to comment. What should Meghna do first?
options: Ignore it to preserve the friendship, since Arjun's work is otherwise good.
Speak to Arjun privately, explain the expectations that apply to the whole team and ask whether something is causing the delays.
Issue Arjun a formal written warning at once to show she has no favourites.
Raise the issue of late arrivals at the next team meeting without naming anyone.
questions.explanation: A private conversation applies the same standard as for everyone while respecting the relationship and uncovering any reason for the delays. Ignoring it erodes her credibility; an immediate formal warning skips a fair first step; a vague team announcement avoids the real issue.

questions.question: A company must reduce headcount in its accounts department by one. Two employees are being considered: Lata, a high performer with two years' service, and Sameer, an average performer with 25 years' service who is due to retire in 18 months and is his family's sole earner. Company policy says reductions should be based on performance. What should the HR head do first?
options: Lay off Lata, because she has the shortest service.
Cancel the headcount reduction to avoid any hardship.
Offer a voluntary retirement package to eligible employees, such as Sameer, before deciding on any forced separation.
Lay off Sameer immediately, as the policy requires.
questions.explanation: A voluntary retirement offer may achieve the reduction humanely, respects Sameer's long service and proximity to retirement, and keeps the stronger performer, consistent with the policy's intent. Laying off Lata ignores policy; an immediate forced exit skips a less harmful option; cancelling ignores the business need.

questions.question: A company's travel policy says: (1) Employees at grade M3 and above may fly business class on flights longer than 4 hours; all others fly economy. (2) Any employee may upgrade at his or her own cost. (3) International travel requires prior approval of the department head; if the employee is travelling with a client, approval of the CFO is also required. Rohit, at grade M2, will fly to Singapore (a 5.5-hour flight) with a client and wants the company to pay for business class. What is the correct position?
options: The company will pay for business class, with approval from the CFO only.
The company will pay only for economy class, with approval from his department head only.
The company will pay for business class, with approval from his department head.
The company will pay only for economy class, and Rohit needs approval from both his department head and the CFO.
questions.explanation: Rule 1: as an M2, Rohit is entitled to economy regardless of flight length (he may upgrade at his own cost under rule 2). Rule 3: international travel with a client needs both the department head's and the CFO's approval.

questions.question:
Four managers—P, Q, R and S—are to be posted, one each, to branches in Delhi, Pune, Kochi and Jaipur.
• The Kochi branch needs a Malayalam speaker; only R and S speak Malayalam.
• P has asked not to be posted to Delhi.
• Q has already served in Pune and cannot return there.
• R cannot be posted to Delhi or Jaipur.
• For family reasons, S can be posted only to Delhi or Kochi.

If S is posted to Delhi, where is Q posted?
options: Delhi
Jaipur
Kochi
Pune
questions.explanation: With S in Delhi, Kochi must go to R (the only other Malayalam speaker). P and Q share Pune and Jaipur; Q cannot go to Pune, so Q goes to Jaipur and P to Pune.

questions.question: A bank's education-loan rules are: (a) loans up to ₹7.5 lakh need no collateral; (b) loans above ₹7.5 lakh need collateral worth at least the loan amount; (c) a parent or guardian must be a co-applicant; (d) students admitted to institutions on the bank's 'Tier A' list get a 0.5 percentage-point interest concession. Neha has been admitted to a Tier A institute and applies for ₹10 lakh with her father as co-applicant, offering a fixed deposit of ₹8 lakh as collateral. What is the most the bank can sanction under these rules, and on what terms?
options: ₹8 lakh, with the 0.5 percentage-point concession
₹7.5 lakh, without any concession
Nothing, since the collateral is less than the amount applied for
₹10 lakh, with the 0.5 percentage-point concession
questions.explanation: Any loan above ₹7.5 lakh needs collateral at least equal to the loan; the ₹8 lakh deposit supports up to ₹8 lakh. The co-applicant condition is met, and the Tier A admission earns the concession. Rejection is unnecessary because a smaller loan satisfies all rules.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Herbert Simon observed decades ago that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. What he could not foresee was an industry organised around harvesting that poverty. Platforms that are free to use are paid, in effect, in minutes of human focus, and they compete by engineering ever more efficient ways to capture it: the infinite scroll, the variable reward of the refreshed feed, the notification timed to the moment of boredom. It is tempting to treat the resulting distraction as a failure of individual willpower. But willpower is a poor defence against systems designed by thousands of engineers to defeat it. To ask a person to resist such design unaided is like asking a swimmer to resist a current that someone has deliberately strengthened."

The author's main contention is that:
options: digital distraction is better understood as a product of deliberate design than as a mere lapse of individual self-control
Simon's observation about information has been disproved by modern platforms
free online platforms should be banned
individuals bear no responsibility at all for how they use technology
questions.explanation: The author argues against blaming willpower because platforms are engineered to capture attention (the strengthened current). The passage builds on Simon rather than refuting him, proposes no ban, and says willpower is a 'poor defence', not that individuals bear no responsibility.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In the gharana tradition, a student of Hindustani music learned not from notation but through years of listening to and imitating a master, often while living in the master's household. Critics charged the system with secrecy and favouritism, and not without reason. Yet the same intimacy allowed the transmission of what notation cannot capture: a characteristic ornament, a way of approaching a note, a sense of when to withhold. Recordings and online lessons have opened the music to anyone with an internet connection. They have also made it easier to copy a master's phrases without absorbing the discipline that gave those phrases their meaning."

With which of the following would the author most likely agree?
options: The gharana system should be revived and recordings of masters withdrawn.
The secrecy of the gharana system served no musical purpose.
Wider access to teaching material does not by itself transmit the deeper discipline that the older system cultivated.
Notation is a superior means of transmitting music than oral learning.
questions.explanation: The final sentences say recordings open access but make it easier to copy phrases 'without absorbing the discipline'. The author concedes the critics' point and never calls for withdrawal of recordings; he says notation cannot capture key elements; and intimacy is credited with a musical purpose.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"If every plank of a ship is replaced over the years, is it still the same ship? Philosophers have argued over the puzzle since antiquity, but companies live it daily. A firm that has replaced its founders, its products, its headquarters and every one of its employees still signs contracts in the same name and is sued for the debts of its past. The law resolves the puzzle by fiat: identity is whatever continuity the registry records. That answer is convenient, but it leaves open whether anything of the original enterprise—its culture, its purpose—survives the replacement of its parts."

The author refers to the ship whose planks are all replaced in order to:
options: argue that companies should never replace their founders
frame a question about what makes an organisation the same over time despite complete change in its components
show that ancient philosophers were interested in shipbuilding
prove that legal identity is the only meaningful form of identity
questions.explanation: The ship puzzle is applied to firms whose every part changes; the passage then contrasts legal identity with cultural continuity. It is a framing device, not about shipbuilding or a prohibition, and the author questions rather than endorses legal identity as the whole answer.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Many teachers believe that students learn better when lessons match their preferred 'learning style'—visual, auditory or kinaesthetic. The idea is intuitive and flattering: it promises that every student can thrive if taught in the right way. Yet when researchers have tested it by teaching students in matched and mismatched styles and measuring what they learned, the predicted advantage has rarely appeared. What does seem to matter is matching the mode to the content: maps are learned best visually and pronunciation by ear, for every student."

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's position?
options: Teachers report that they enjoy preparing lessons in several styles.
A large controlled study found that students taught in their self-reported preferred style scored significantly higher than equally able students taught in a mismatched style.
Most students learn geography better from maps than from spoken descriptions.
Most students, when asked, can name a preferred learning style.
questions.explanation: The author's position is that style-matching shows no real benefit. A rigorous study showing matched students learning more directly contradicts that. Stated preferences and teacher enjoyment do not show learning gains; the map finding supports the author's content-matching view.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Gandhi's idea of trusteeship asked the wealthy to regard their surplus not as private property but as a trust held for the community, to be used for the common good. Critics on the left saw it as naive, a way of leaving property untouched while waiting for a change of heart that would never come. Critics on the right saw it as an attack on ownership dressed in moral language. Both readings may be correct about its weaknesses. But the idea's near-total disappearance from public debate may say less about its merits than about our impatience with any proposal that depends on moral transformation rather than on law."

Which of the following best expresses the author's view of trusteeship?
options: Its neglect may reflect discomfort with moral rather than legal remedies as much as any flaw in the idea itself.
It is superior to every legal form of redistribution.
It was a disguised defence of the property of the rich.
It was rejected chiefly because it could not be enforced in court.
questions.explanation: The author grants the critics' points about weaknesses but suggests the idea's disappearance reflects 'impatience' with moral rather than legal approaches. The second option is one critic's reading; enforceability is not given as the reason; the author makes no claim of superiority.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The stepwells of western India were not merely sources of water. Descending in tiers to the water table, they kept water within reach as its level rose and fell with the seasons, and their shaded galleries were cool gathering places in summer. Colonial engineers, judging them unhygienic, replaced many with piped supply and hand pumps. The new systems were cleaner, but they drew on deeper aquifers, and as stepwells fell into disuse, so did the local practice of channelling monsoon run-off into them. Several cities now spend heavily on rainwater-harvesting schemes that rediscover, at great expense, what the stepwells did for centuries."

It can be inferred that the author regards modern rainwater-harvesting schemes as:
options: in part a costly rediscovery of functions that traditional structures once performed
unnecessary, since piped water supply meets all needs
less hygienic than the stepwells they replaced
a direct continuation of colonial water policy
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the schemes 'rediscover, at great expense, what the stepwells did for centuries'. Nothing calls them unnecessary or colonial in origin, and hygiene is discussed only for stepwells versus piped supply.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Tax authorities in several countries have tried a simple experiment: letters to late payers that mention that most people in their town have already paid. Such letters raised payment rates more than letters that merely restated the penalty for late payment. Letters that described taxes as paying for local hospitals and schools had smaller, but still noticeable, effects. Nudges of this kind are cheap and often effective. But they work at the margins; they cannot rescue a tax system that people believe to be unfair."

According to the passage, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Messages linking taxes to public services had some positive effect.
Information about other people's behaviour can influence tax compliance.
A perception of unfairness can limit the effect of nudges.
Letters restating the penalty for late payment were more effective than letters citing other people's compliance.
questions.explanation: The passage says letters citing neighbours' compliance raised payment 'more than letters that merely restated the penalty'—the opposite of the first option. The other three are stated in the passage.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Boredom has a poor reputation; we treat it as a waste of time to be filled as quickly as possible. Yet psychologists who made volunteers perform a dull task before a creative one found that the bored volunteers produced more original ideas than those who had not been bored. Boredom, on this view, is a signal—an uncomfortable push to look for something more meaningful than what is in front of us. The trouble with the smartphone is not that it entertains us. It is that it silences the signal before the signal can do its work."

The author's concern about smartphones is that they:
options: make people less intelligent over time
relieve boredom so readily that its prompting towards more meaningful activity is lost
cause boredom by presenting dull content
are too entertaining to be used for serious work
questions.explanation: The author calls boredom a useful signal and says the smartphone 'silences the signal before the signal can do its work'. The passage explicitly says the problem is not entertainment itself; it does not claim phones cause boredom or reduce intelligence.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Companies increasingly promise to become 'carbon neutral' by buying offsets—payments for planting trees or protecting forests elsewhere to balance emissions they cannot yet cut. The logic depends on two conditions. The forest protected must actually have been at risk; paying to preserve a forest that no one planned to cut buys nothing. And the carbon stored must stay stored; a plantation that burns in a drought returns its carbon to the air. Audits of several offset schemes have found one condition, or both, unmet."

Which of the following, if true, would most undermine a company's claim to be carbon neutral through an offset it purchased?
options: The company plans to reduce its own emissions further over the next decade.
The forest it paid to protect is home to several endangered bird species.
The company's offset payments were made through an international broker.
The forest it paid to protect lies inside a national park where logging was already prohibited and effectively enforced.
questions.explanation: If logging was already prohibited and enforced, the forest was not at risk, so the payment 'buys nothing'—failing the first condition. Biodiversity, the use of a broker and future reduction plans do not affect whether the offset is real.

questions.question:
"Data from our city show that neighbourhoods with more police stations also report more crimes. Police stations evidently attract crime, so the city should stop building new ones."

Which of the following best identifies the flaw in this reasoning?
options: It ignores the likelihood that police stations are built where crime is already high.
It assumes that all crimes are reported to the police.
It does not state how many police stations the city has.
It relies on data from a single city.
questions.explanation: The argument treats a correlation as proof that stations cause crime, overlooking reversed causation: more stations are placed in high-crime areas. The other points are minor or irrelevant to the conclusion.

questions.question:
"After a chain of cafés introduced free Wi-Fi, the average time each customer spent in its outlets rose by 25%. Management concluded that the Wi-Fi has increased the chain's revenue."

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens management's conclusion?
options: Competing cafés also offer free Wi-Fi.
Many customers said they liked having free Wi-Fi.
Average spending per visit rose along with time spent, while the number of customers turned away for lack of seats did not increase.
Customers who use Wi-Fi often occupy a table for several hours.
questions.explanation: Longer stays raise revenue only if customers spend more and the extra time does not block other paying customers. The first option establishes both. Customer approval and competitors' Wi-Fi do not show revenue gains, and long table occupancy could reduce revenue.

questions.question:
"Every employee who completed the advanced analytics course was promoted this year. No one in the Pune office was promoted this year. Ritu works in the Pune office."

Which of the following must be true?
options: No one in the Pune office was eligible for the course.
Ritu did not complete the advanced analytics course.
Some employees in the Pune office completed the course.
Ritu will be promoted next year.
questions.explanation: Ritu was not promoted (no one in Pune was). Completing the course guarantees promotion, so she cannot have completed it. Eligibility, next year and the other Pune employees are not determined; in fact no Pune employee can have completed the course.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Choose the most logical order.

1. Within a generation, the grand houses stood empty or had been turned into godowns, and the merchant families had moved north.
2. The port city grew rich on the spice trade, and its merchants built grand houses near the waterfront.
3. When steamships made the deeper harbour to the north more convenient, trade shifted there almost overnight.
4. Today those buildings are being converted into cafés and galleries for tourists who come to see the old city.
questions.explanation: 2 introduces the prosperous port and its houses; 3 explains the shift of trade; 1 describes the consequence ('within a generation'); 4 ('those buildings', 'today') brings the story to the present.

questions.question:
Five sentences are given below. Four of them form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does NOT belong.

1. The printing press made books cheaper, but it also made errors more durable.
2. A scribe's mistake affected a single manuscript; a misprint was reproduced in every copy of an edition.
3. Printers responded by employing correctors, who checked proofs against the author's manuscript before a full run.
4. Paper mills had spread across much of Europe well before printing arrived.
5. Lists of errata, printed at the back of books, were an admission of the mistakes that still slipped through.
options: Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 5
Sentence 2
questions.explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 concern how printing multiplied errors and how printers tried to correct them. Sentence 4, about the spread of paper mills, shares the period but not the thread of errors.

questions.question:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.

"The management's ______ proposals, which conceded nothing of substance, did little to ______ the striking workers."
options: cosmetic … placate
substantive … pacify
sweeping … mollify
token … antagonise
questions.explanation: Proposals that 'conceded nothing of substance' are cosmetic, and such proposals would fail to placate (calm) strikers. 'Substantive' and 'sweeping' contradict the first clause; 'did little to antagonise' makes no sense as the expected effect.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Hardly had the meeting began when the power failed.
Hardly the meeting had begun when the power failed.
Hardly had the meeting begun when the power failed.
Hardly had the meeting begun than the power failed.
questions.explanation: A sentence opening with 'Hardly' takes inversion ('had the meeting begun'), is followed by 'when' (not 'than'), and uses the past participle 'begun'.

questions.question:
Read the poem and answer the question.

"My grandmother kept her recipes
in no book. They lived in her wrists—
the turn that knew when dough was ready,
the pinch that was never a measure.
We wrote them down after she died:
cups, spoons, minutes, degrees.
We cooked exactly what she taught us,
and it was nothing like hers."

Which of the following best captures the central idea of the poem?
options: Some knowledge lives in practised touch and judgement and is lost when reduced to written measurement.
Written recipes are always inaccurate and should not be used.
The grandmother deliberately kept her recipes secret from her family.
The family did not follow the written recipes carefully enough.
questions.explanation: The recipes 'lived in her wrists'—embodied skill—and the written version, though followed 'exactly', fails to reproduce her cooking. The poem says they cooked exactly as taught, implies no secrecy, and makes no general claim about all written recipes.

questions.question: A trader buys goods at a 20% discount on the list price and sells them at 10% above the list price. What is his profit percentage?
questions.explanation: On a list price of 100, cost = 80 and selling price = 110. Profit = 30/80 = 37.5%.

questions.question: Two cyclists start at the same time from towns A and B, 60 km apart, and ride towards each other at 12 km/h and 18 km/h. At the same moment, a bird starts from the first cyclist and flies at 30 km/h back and forth between the two cyclists until they meet. What total distance does the bird fly?
options: 72 km
50 km
90 km
60 km
questions.explanation: The cyclists close the gap at 30 km/h and meet after 60/30 = 2 hours. The bird flies for 2 hours at 30 km/h: 60 km.

questions.question: A can finish a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. In how many days will the job be completed?
questions.explanation: Every two days they complete 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12. After 22 days, 11/12 is done. Day 23 (A) adds 1/20, making 58/60; day 24 (B) adds 2/60, completing the job.

questions.question: How many litres of a 30% acid solution must be added to 20 litres of a 60% acid solution to obtain a 50% acid solution?
questions.explanation: By alligation, the 30% and 60% solutions must be mixed in the ratio (60 − 50) : (50 − 30) = 1 : 2. With 20 litres of the 60% solution, 10 litres of the 30% solution are needed.

questions.question: A sum lent at simple interest amounts to ₹7,200 in 3 years and to ₹8,400 in 5 years. What is the rate of interest per annum?
If a + b + c = 0 and a, b, c are non-zero, what is the value of a²/(bc) + b²/(ca) + c²/(ab)?
questions.explanation: The expression equals (a³ + b³ + c³)/(abc). When a + b + c = 0, a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc, so the value is 3.

questions.question: How many ordered triples of positive odd integers (x, y, z) satisfy x + y + z = 15?
questions.explanation: Write x = 2a + 1, y = 2b + 1, z = 2c + 1 with a, b, c ≥ 0. Then 2(a + b + c) = 12, so a + b + c = 6, which has C(8, 2) = 28 non-negative solutions.

questions.question: Let f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 1) for x ≠ 1. What is the value of f(f(f(3)))?
The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression is 3n² + 5n. What is its 10th term?
In triangle ABC, AB = 12 cm, AC = 8 cm and BC = 15 cm. The bisector of angle A meets BC at D. What is the length of BD?
options: 7.5 cm
9 cm
10 cm
6 cm
questions.explanation: By the angle-bisector theorem, BD : DC = AB : AC = 12 : 8 = 3 : 2. BD = 15 × 3/5 = 9 cm.

questions.question: What is the distance between the parallel lines 3x + 4y = 7 and 6x + 8y = −6?
questions.explanation: Rewrite the second line as 3x + 4y = −3. Distance = |7 − (−3)|/√(3² + 4²) = 10/5 = 2. Using the unscaled equations gives the wrong value 13/10 = 1.3.

questions.question: A right circular cone has a base radius of 7 cm and a height of 24 cm. What is its curved surface area? (Take π = 22/7.)
options: 528 cm²
616 cm²
550 cm²
704 cm²
questions.explanation: Slant height = √(7² + 24²) = 25 cm. Curved surface area = πrl = (22/7) × 7 × 25 = 550 cm².

questions.question: What is the units digit of 3²⁰²⁶ × 7²⁰²⁵?
questions.explanation: Units digits of powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1; 2026 ≡ 2 (mod 4) gives 9. Powers of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1; 2025 ≡ 1 (mod 4) gives 7. 9 × 7 = 63, units digit 3.

questions.question: The product of two natural numbers is 2,160 and their HCF is 12. How many such pairs of numbers are there (unordered)?
questions.explanation: Write the numbers as 12m and 12n with m, n coprime. 144mn = 2,160 gives mn = 15. Coprime pairs: (1, 15) and (3, 5). So 2 pairs: (12, 180) and (36, 60).

questions.question: In how many ways can 5 men and 4 women sit in a row so that no two women sit next to each other?
questions.explanation: Arrange the men: 5! = 120. They create 6 gaps; choose and arrange the women in 4 of them: P(6, 4) = 360. Total = 120 × 360 = 43,200.

questions.question: A box contains 4 red and 5 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are of the same colour?
questions.explanation: Same colour: C(4,2) + C(5,2) = 6 + 10 = 16 out of C(9,2) = 36. Probability = 16/36 = 4/9. (41/81 would be the answer with replacement.)

questions.question:
A company's revenue and total expenditure (₹ crore) were:

Year | Revenue | Expenditure
2022 | 250 | 200
2023 | 300 | 234
2024 | 360 | 288
2025 | 400 | 316

In which year was the profit margin (profit as a percentage of revenue) the highest?
questions.explanation: Profit margins: 2022 50/250 = 20%; 2023 66/300 = 22%; 2024 72/360 = 20%; 2025 84/400 = 21%. 2023 is highest, although 2025 had the largest absolute profit.

questions.question: In an examination taken by 120 students, 45% passed in Mathematics, 60% passed in English and 25% passed in both. How many students failed in both subjects?
questions.explanation: Passed at least one = 45% + 60% − 25% = 80%. Failed both = 20% of 120 = 24.

questions.question: Who became Japan's first woman Prime Minister in October 2025?
options: Sanae Takaichi
Shigeru Ishiba
Seiko Noda
Yuriko Koike
questions.explanation: Sanae Takaichi was elected leader of the Liberal Democratic Party and became Prime Minister in October 2025, succeeding Shigeru Ishiba.

questions.question: The 2025 Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to:
options: Jon Fosse
Han Kang
Annie Ernaux
László Krasznahorkai
questions.explanation: The Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai won the 2025 prize. Han Kang (2024), Jon Fosse (2023) and Annie Ernaux (2022) were the previous laureates.

questions.question: Which Indian city was chosen in November 2025 to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games?
options: New Delhi
Bhubaneswar
Ahmedabad
Hyderabad
questions.explanation: Commonwealth Sport's General Assembly awarded the 2030 Games—the centenary edition—to Ahmedabad. New Delhi hosted the 2010 Games.

questions.question: 'Heart Lamp', the story collection that won the International Booker Prize in 2025, was originally written in which language?
options: Urdu
Kannada
Malayalam
Tamil
questions.explanation: Banu Mushtaq's 'Heart Lamp', translated by Deepa Bhasthi, was originally written in Kannada; it was the first Kannada work to win the prize.

questions.question: Who became Chancellor of Germany in May 2025?
options: Christian Lindner
Friedrich Merz
Olaf Scholz
Annalena Baerbock
questions.explanation: Friedrich Merz of the CDU was elected Chancellor by the Bundestag in May 2025, succeeding Olaf Scholz.

questions.question: María Corina Machado, awarded the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, is an opposition leader from which country?
options: Belarus
Nicaragua
Colombia
Venezuela
questions.explanation: The Norwegian Nobel Committee honoured María Corina Machado for her work promoting democratic rights in Venezuela.

questions.question: Vistara, which was merged into Air India in November 2024, was a joint venture between Tata Sons and which airline?
options: Lufthansa
Emirates
Qatar Airways
Singapore Airlines
questions.explanation: Vistara was a Tata Sons–Singapore Airlines joint venture; after the merger Singapore Airlines took a stake of about 25% in Air India.

questions.question: Under the new income-tax regime announced in the Union Budget 2025–26, no income tax is payable by a resident individual on income (excluding special-rate income) of up to:
options: ₹10 lakh
₹7 lakh
₹15 lakh
₹12 lakh
questions.explanation: Budget 2025–26 raised the rebate so that income up to ₹12 lakh attracts no tax under the new regime (₹12.75 lakh for salaried taxpayers after the standard deduction). ₹7 lakh was the earlier threshold.

questions.question: The Battle of Plassey, which laid the foundation of British political power in Bengal, was fought in:
questions.explanation: Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey in 1757. Buxar was in 1764 and the third battle of Panipat in 1761.

questions.question: Which is the longest river of peninsular India?
options: Krishna
Mahanadi
Narmada
Godavari
questions.explanation: The Godavari, about 1,465 km long, is the longest river of peninsular India and is often called the 'Dakshin Ganga'.

questions.question: What is the minimum age prescribed by the Constitution of India for a person to be a member of the Rajya Sabha?
options: 35 years
21 years
30 years
25 years
questions.explanation: Article 84 prescribes a minimum age of 30 years for the Rajya Sabha and 25 years for the Lok Sabha.

questions.question: The Thomas Cup, which India won for the first time in 2022, is a world team championship in which sport?
options: Tennis
Badminton
Squash
Table tennis
questions.explanation: The Thomas Cup is the men's world team badminton championship; India beat Indonesia in the 2022 final in Bangkok.
